analysis.one_liner: Requires insurance plans to charge the same for oral cancer pills as for IV chemotherapy.
analysis.headline: The bill, with bipartisan sponsors from four states, never left the Senate committee it was sent to and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Many newer cancer medicines are pills patients take at home, but health plans often charge much more for pills than for chemotherapy dripped into a vein at a clinic. This bill would require any plan that covers IV or injected cancer drugs to give oral cancer drugs equally favorable copays, deductibles, and coinsurance. It also bars insurers from dodging the rule by raising costs or adding new restrictions on oral drugs, and it applies even to older 'grandfathered' plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Cancer patients whose doctors prescribe oral anticancer drugs, who currently can face far higher out-of-pocket costs than patients receiving IV chemotherapy; plans must price the pill and the IV on the same terms.

how_it_helps.text: Plans covering IV or injected anticancer drugs must apply cost sharing (deductible, coinsurance, copay, and out-of-pocket maximums) to patient-administered oral anticancer drugs on terms no less favorable than for IV/injected drugs, so patients who take pills at home do not pay more than patients who get an infusion at a clinic.

The rule applies to FDA-approved drugs a physician finds medically necessary or clinically appropriate, and the bill blocks plans from complying by raising out-of-pocket costs, reclassifying benefits, or applying stricter limits to oral drugs.
The requirement extends to grandfathered health plans, so older plans cannot keep charging higher cost sharing for oral chemotherapy.
States with stronger protections keep them, since the federal rule is a floor, not a ceiling.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and issuers, who would lose the ability to shift higher cost sharing onto patients choosing oral chemotherapy; the added coverage could raise plan costs modestly, which may be passed into premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and group health plans

drawbacks.text: Equalizing cost sharing would increase what insurers pay for oral cancer drugs, and some of that cost could show up in premiums for all enrollees; the bill does not cap drug prices, only how their cost is split.
Plans may keep prior authorization and other utilization controls on any chemotherapy, so equal cost sharing does not guarantee quick access to oral drugs.

The rule only requires parity where a plan covers IV anticancer drugs at all, and does not set an absolute dollar cap, so patients still face whatever cost sharing the plan imposes in the first place.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete and targeted: patients whose doctors prescribe pills can keep taking them without paying hundreds or thousands more than infusion patients. The cost is higher drug coverage spending by insurers, some of which may reach premiums, and the bill does nothing about the underlying prices of cancer drugs. On balance it is a consumer-protection fix with a modest, diffuse cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate on December 12, 2018, read twice, and sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it stayed until the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019 — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the Cancer Drug Parity Act of 2018 with Sens. Moran, Murphy, and Wicker as original cosponsors, giving it sponsorship from both parties.
On the day of introduction the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions; the action history shows no further action.
Five senators cosponsored the bill — two Republicans and three Democrats — but the committee never took it up and no vote ever occurred before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health plans and insurers are better off, since they can keep charging higher copays and coinsurance for oral anticancer drugs than for IV chemotherapy. Cancer patients who take pills at home continue to pay the difference, while patients in states with their own parity laws already had protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers charging more for cancer pills

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start: one Democrat introduced it with two Republican and one Democratic original cosponsors, and the full five cosponsors split 3 Democrats and 2 Republicans; no one acted against it on the record — it simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Health insurers and group health plans
industries.note: The bill would end their ability to price oral cancer pills less favorably than IV chemotherapy, cutting cost-sharing revenue and shifting more drug costs onto premiums for everyone. Patients who need pills would pay less.

By making oral chemotherapy no more expensive to the patient than infusions, the bill could increase uptake of oral cancer drugs, many of which are high-priced specialty products. It does not address drug prices themselves, so patients get affordability at the pharmacy counter while the drug companies keep their prices.

Parity removes the price penalty that steered some patients toward clinic-administered chemotherapy, so some treatment could shift away from infusion settings toward home pills. The bill expressly does not require anyone to switch from IV to oral drugs.
